title: The whirlwind
hookLine: God answers with stars, sea and wild animals, not with a reason (Job 38–39)

cards: What would you say if you finally got the meeting? Job has had chapter after chapter to prepare. He has his case and his arguments, and he has waited.

Then, after all the talking, the voice he's been asking for arrives, and not quietly. "Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind." What comes back from the storm is a long list of questions of its own.

teach.b: First, questions for questions. The very first thing God asks: "Where wast thou when I laid the foundations of the earth? declare, if thou hast understanding." Not an accusation of sin; a question about scale.

Second, stars and sea. The questions keep coming, and they're beautiful. Where was Job when the earth's cornerstone was laid, "When the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy?"
Who shut in the sea and told it: "Hitherto shalt thou come, but no further: and here shall thy proud waves be stayed"? Can you bind the Pleiades, or loosen the bands of Orion?
Third, animals nobody tamed. The wild donkey who laughs at the noise of the city. The wild ox who won't be harnessed.
The ostrich. The war horse: "hast thou clothed his neck with thunder?" The hawk: "Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, and stretch her wings toward the south?"
A whole world going about its business with no human in charge of it.

teach.h: NO REASON, AND STILL AN ANSWER.
teach.b: Fourth, no reason, and still an answer. God never mentions the scene in heaven from chapter one. Job is never told why.
And yet his reply, near the end, is this: "I have heard of thee by the hearing of the ear: but now mine eye seeth thee." Readers have heard the whirlwind in different ways.
Some hear a rebuke, putting Job in his place. Some hear comfort, that the world is held by someone bigger than the question. Some hear an invitation out of the ash heap and into a much wider world.
The book doesn't settle it. It answers the argument by showing Job the world.

how: Jews and Christians read God's speeches from the whirlwind in Job 38–41 as scripture, and interpret them differently: as rebuke, as comfort, or as a widening of Job's view.

games.q: you're Job. you've demanded a hearing, and God answers you out of the whirlwind. what do you hear first?
o: a question: where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth?
games.why: God answers with questions about creation, stars, sea and wild animals, and never gives the reason.

practice: Find something wild to look at, a tree, a bird, the sky through a window; if not, a houseplant, or your own breath, which goes on without your permission.
Let it be bigger than your questions for now, and notice that it doesn't need you to run it. If a question about your own life comes up, let it sit alongside the wild thing, not on top of it.
